cards.heading: Why connections are expensive
cards.hook: Opening a new PostgreSQL connection costs 50 to 200 milliseconds before a single query even runs.
cards.body: That's a TCP handshake, SSL negotiation, authentication, and a forked backend process — paid again on every request that opens its own connection.

cards.heading: What a connection pool actually is
cards.hook: A pool keeps connections open and ready, so a request borrows one and returns it instead of paying setup cost every time.
cards.code:
const pool = new Pool({ max: 20, min: 5 });
// borrow -> query -> release, instead of opening fresh each time

cards.heading: Sizing a pool
cards.hook: Pool size is roughly cores times two, plus disk spindles — two to four times cores for a typical I/O-bound web app.
cards.body: More connections past that point doesn't mean more speed, it means memory pressure and lock contention.
cards.code: max = (cpu_cores * 2) + disk_spindles

cards.heading: Idle and acquire timeouts matter
cards.hook: idleTimeoutMillis closes connections nobody's using; connectionTimeoutMillis decides how long a request waits before failing instead of queueing forever.
cards.code:
idleTimeoutMillis: 30000,
connectionTimeoutMillis: 2000

cards.heading: PgBouncer sits between app and database
cards.hook: Three app instances can each open a hundred connections while PostgreSQL only ever sees a fraction of them.
cards.body: PgBouncer multiplexes many client connections onto a small shared pool of real database ones.

cards.heading: Transaction mode is the one to pick
cards.hook: PgBouncer's transaction mode returns a connection the moment a transaction commits, not when the client disconnects.
cards.body: That's what lets a handful of real connections serve thousands of app-side ones — session mode exists mainly for compatibility.

cards.heading: One process per connection
cards.hook: PostgreSQL forks a whole OS process per connection instead of using threads — five to ten megabytes of overhead, but a crash in one never touches another.

cards.heading: The hot row problem
cards.hook: A thousand concurrent purchases on one popular product can serialize down to a few hundred updates a second.
cards.body: Every UPDATE needs an exclusive lock on that exact row, so the rest just queue behind it.

cards.heading: Fixing hot row contention
cards.hook: SKIP LOCKED, optimistic locking with a version column, or an async stock update — pick one before a hot row becomes your bottleneck.

cards.heading: Write ahead, then acknowledge
cards.hook: PostgreSQL writes every change to the log and flushes it to disk before telling the client the commit succeeded.
cards.body: The actual data pages get updated lazily afterward — that order is what makes crash recovery possible.

cards.heading: Why MVCC needs a cleanup crew
cards.hook: An UPDATE never overwrites a row — it leaves the old version as a dead tuple and writes a fresh one.
cards.body: A heavily updated table that's never vacuumed just keeps growing with rows nobody can even see anymore.

cards.heading: Watch pool usage, not just query time
cards.hook: A pool's idle and waiting counts reveal requests queueing for a connection before a single query even starts.
cards.code: console.log(pool.totalCount, pool.idleCount, pool.waitingCount);

cards.heading: What an index buys you
cards.hook: No index means every query scans every row. The right index turns a million-row scan into about twenty comparisons.

cards.heading: What a b-tree index can't do
cards.hook: A b-tree handles equality, ranges, and a prefix LIKE search just fine — a suffix wildcard or full text search needs a different index type entirely.

cards.heading: The leftmost prefix rule
cards.hook: A composite index on (user_id, status) works for user_id alone or both together — but never for status alone.

cards.heading: A covering index skips the table entirely
cards.hook: If an index already holds every column a query needs, PostgreSQL never touches the table — the fastest a read can possibly be.
cards.code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_covering ON orders (user_id, status, total);

cards.heading: Partial indexes for the rows you actually query
cards.hook: Indexing only the pending orders gives you a far smaller index that stays fast even as the ignored rows pile up.
cards.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending ON orders (created_at)
WHERE status = 'PENDING';

cards.heading: A function on a column needs its own index
cards.hook: WHERE LOWER(email) = ... can't use a plain index on email — the fix is indexing the expression itself.
cards.code: CREATE INDEX idx_users_lower_email ON users (LOWER(email));

cards.heading: Every index costs on writes
cards.hook: Every index gets updated on every INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE — indexing everything quietly slows down writes for reads that may never happen.

cards.heading: Implicit type conversion disables an index
cards.hook: Comparing an indexed int column to a string parameter can force PostgreSQL to convert every row before comparing — silently skipping the index.

cards.heading: Column order in a composite index matters
cards.hook: Put the column you always filter on first. Get the order backwards and half your queries can't use the index, even with the right columns in it.

cards.heading: UPSERT in one statement
cards.hook: ON CONFLICT turns a check-then-insert-or-update dance into one atomic round trip to the database.
cards.code:
INSERT INTO product_views (product_id, user_id, count)
VALUES ($1, $2, 1)
ON CONFLICT (product_id, user_id)
DO UPDATE SET count = product_views.count + 1;

cards.heading: Recursive CTEs walk a hierarchy
cards.hook: A recursive CTE feeds its own output back into itself until a round produces nothing new — exactly how you walk an org chart or category tree.
cards.code:
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, 1 AS depth FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1
  FROM employees e JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT * FROM org_chart;

cards.heading: Window functions rank without collapsing rows
cards.hook: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK rank rows within a group while still returning one row per input — unlike GROUP BY, which collapses the group.
cards.code: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC)

cards.heading: A running total with one window function
cards.hook: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date) turns a grand total into a running total — no self join, no subquery.

cards.heading: ROLLUP computes several totals in one pass
cards.hook: GROUP BY ROLLUP gives you per-city, per-country, and grand totals from one query instead of three.
cards.code: GROUP BY ROLLUP (country, city)

cards.heading: A materialized view trades freshness for speed
cards.hook: A materialized view stores its result physically on disk and only updates when you REFRESH it — perfect for an expensive daily rollup nobody needs to the second.

cards.heading: Triggers keep derived data in sync
cards.hook: A trigger runs inside the same transaction as the change that caused it, so derived data can never drift out of sync.

cards.heading: Full text search needs its own index type
cards.hook: to_tsvector turns a column into a searchable document; a GIN index on it is what makes the search fast instead of a full scan.

cards.heading: Row level security filters rows per user
cards.hook: Enable RLS and attach a policy, and every query is automatically filtered to only the rows that policy allows — even if application code forgets to.

cards.heading: Parameterized queries are not optional
cards.hook: Interpolating a request parameter into a SQL string is an injection waiting to happen — a parameterized query can never be read as SQL.

cards.heading: pg_trgm turns typos into matches
cards.hook: Index a column with pg_trgm and a search for jhon matches john by trigram similarity, not exact text.

cards.heading: The psql commands worth memorizing
cards.hook: \dt lists tables, \d plus a name describes one, and \x unwraps a wide row into one field per line.
cards.code:
\dt          -- list tables
\d orders    -- describe a table
\x           -- toggle expanded display

cards.heading: pg_dump backs up without locking
cards.hook: pg_dump snapshots a database without blocking reads or writes, and its custom format restores in parallel with pg_restore for real speed.

cards.heading: JSONB supports real queries, not just storage
cards.hook: The containment operator plus a GIN index lets you query inside a jsonb column fast — not just store it.
cards.code: SELECT * FROM events WHERE data @> '{"action": "login"}';

cards.heading: The planner guesses, it does not know
cards.hook: Stale statistics let the planner confidently pick a sequential scan over ten million rows it believes are a thousand.

cards.heading: Reading cost numbers in EXPLAIN
cards.hook: Startup cost and total cost are an arbitrary unit for comparing plans — never a prediction of real wall-clock time.

cards.heading: The real red flag in EXPLAIN ANALYZE
cards.hook: Estimated 5 rows, actual 50,000? The planner worked off bad information — run ANALYZE and fix it.

cards.heading: Rows removed by filter is wasted work
cards.hook: An index that narrows rows, followed by a filter applied after, means PostgreSQL fetched rows the index couldn't screen on its own.
cards.body: Folding the filtered column into one composite index removes that wasted work entirely.
cards.code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders (status, created_at);

cards.heading: The N+1 query problem
cards.hook: Fetch a thousand orders, then query each one's items separately, and two queries just became a thousand and one.
cards.body: A single JOIN would have returned the exact same data in one round trip.

cards.heading: OFFSET pagination gets slower every page
cards.hook: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 9980 scans and discards 9980 rows before returning anything — page 500 pays for every page before it.

cards.heading: Cursor pagination stays flat at any depth
cards.hook: Remember the last row you saw and ask for rows after it — page one and page one thousand both take five milliseconds.
cards.code: WHERE created_at < $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20

cards.heading: SELECT star costs more than it looks
cards.hook: SELECT * fetches columns you don't need and breaks the day someone adds one you weren't expecting.

cards.heading: COUNT(*) on a huge table is slow by design
cards.hook: PostgreSQL keeps no maintained row count — COUNT(*) on a big table means scanning every row of it.

cards.heading: UPSERT removes a race condition
cards.hook: Check-then-insert leaves a window where two requests both see no row and both try to insert — ON CONFLICT makes the check and the write atomic.

cards.heading: Let the slow query log find problems for you
cards.hook: Set log_min_duration_statement to 100ms, and every slow query logs itself before a user ever complains.

cards.heading: Diagnose before you scale
cards.hook: Too many reads needs a read replica. Too many writes needs sharding. Reaching for the wrong one fixes nothing.

cards.heading: Synchronous vs asynchronous replication
cards.hook: Synchronous replication waits for a replica to confirm before committing — zero data loss, more latency.
cards.body: Asynchronous replication commits immediately and lets replicas catch up afterward, trading a little safety for speed.

cards.heading: Replication lag is the hidden problem
cards.hook: A write on the primary isn't instantly visible on a replica — a user reading their own change right after can see it missing.
cards.body: The fix is routing that user's next read back to the primary for a short window.

cards.heading: What belongs on a replica vs the primary
cards.hook: Reports and dashboards belong on a replica. A balance check right after a transfer belongs on the primary.

cards.heading: Sharding splits writes across servers
cards.hook: A read replica only helps reads. Sharding partitions the data itself so writes scale horizontally too.
cards.body: The cost is that the application now has to know which shard holds which row.

cards.heading: Hash sharding spreads load evenly
cards.hook: Hash a key like user_id across N shards and load spreads evenly, with no hot shard.
cards.body: But a range query like last week's orders now has to fan out to every single shard.

cards.heading: Cross-shard queries break the rules
cards.hook: A query touching two shards loses the single database's join and ACID guarantees — the biggest reason teams delay sharding as long as possible.

cards.heading: Partitioning is sharding without leaving one server
cards.hook: Range-partition a table by month, and dropping an old one is instant — not a slow, table-locking DELETE.

cards.heading: Partition pruning skips irrelevant data
cards.hook: Filter on the partition key, and PostgreSQL works out at plan time which partitions can't possibly match — and skips them entirely.

cards.heading: Vertical scaling has a ceiling
cards.hook: A bigger server needs zero app changes but tops out at the biggest machine your cloud sells.

cards.heading: The real choice is CP or AP
cards.hook: Network partitions happen no matter how well you build — so a distributed database either errors out to stay consistent, or answers with stale data to stay available.

cards.heading: Pick CP for money, AP for everything else
cards.hook: A stale balance is a financial bug — go CP. A stale like count costs nothing — go AP and stay available.

cards.heading: MVP schemas optimize for change
cards.hook: Under ten thousand users, the simplest normalized schema you can write is the right one.
cards.body: A wrong guess about future scale costs more than a slow query nobody has hit yet.

cards.heading: One index fixes the first real slow query
cards.hook: A category filter sorted by date turns into a sequential scan past about a hundred thousand rows.
cards.body: One composite index on both columns, in that order, fixes it with zero code changes.

cards.heading: Denormalize only once a join actually hurts
cards.hook: A maintained item_count column turned a 200ms join into a 5ms flat read.
cards.body: Worth the small trigger overhead only because reads vastly outnumbered writes here.

cards.heading: A leading wildcard can't use an index
cards.hook: %laptop% forces a full scan. A tsvector column with a GIN index took the same search from 800ms to 20.

cards.heading: Event sourcing decouples writes from side effects
cards.hook: Append one event row with every relevant detail embedded, and a background worker can send the notification off the critical path entirely.

cards.heading: EAV turns every query into a self join
cards.hook: Storing every attribute as entity, name, value avoids ever changing the schema — but a two-attribute lookup means joining the same table to itself.

cards.heading: Polymorphic foreign keys can't be enforced
cards.hook: The database can never verify a polymorphic reference exists — delete a photo and its comments silently orphan.

cards.heading: A random UUID fragments a write-heavy table
cards.hook: A random UUID has no relation to insert order, so every insert lands in a random spot in the index — constant page splits.
cards.body: Keep a sequential BIGSERIAL as the real key and expose UUID only for external APIs.
cards.code:
id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
external_id UUID NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()

cards.heading: NOT NULL with a default locks a huge table
cards.hook: Adding it directly to a 100M row table rewrites the whole thing under lock — hours of downtime.
cards.body: Add nullable, backfill in batches, then add the constraint, and the lock never happens.

cards.heading: Hot vs cold data tiering
cards.hook: Most queries only touch the last few weeks, even when a table holds years of history.
cards.body: Moving old partitions to cheaper storage keeps the hot set small without deleting anything anyone still needs.

cards.heading: Never rename a column directly
cards.hook: Renaming in place breaks any code still using the old name mid-deploy.
cards.body: Add the new column, copy the data, deploy, then drop the old one once nothing references it.

cards.heading: NUMERIC for money, never FLOAT
cards.hook: Floating point stores an approximation — two numbers that look equal can silently fail to match.
cards.body: NUMERIC stores the exact decimal digits, which is why every schema touching money should use it.

cards.heading: TIMESTAMPTZ, not TIMESTAMP
cards.hook: TIMESTAMPTZ stores a real moment in time and converts it per session's timezone.
cards.body: Plain TIMESTAMP is a timezone-less value that quietly means something different depending on where it's read.

cards.heading: Soft deletes trade a clean query for an audit trail
cards.hook: A deleted_at column preserves data and keeps foreign keys intact, but every query now has to filter it.
cards.body: A partial index on deleted_at IS NULL keeps those filtered queries fast.
cards.code: CREATE INDEX idx_users_active_email ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

cards.heading: JSONB is for variable data, not laziness
cards.hook: A field you always query by belongs in a real column, even if JSONB would technically work.

cards.heading: Safe migrations never lock production for long
cards.hook: A nullable column is always safe. CONCURRENTLY avoids locking on a new index.
cards.body: A NOT NULL column with a default on a big table is the one thing that's never safe to run directly.

cards.heading: A naming scheme that reads like documentation
cards.hook: snake_case plural tables, {table}_id for foreign keys, idx_{table}_{columns} for indexes — anyone can guess the right name without opening the schema.

cards.heading: Audit columns belong on every table from day one
cards.hook: created_at, updated_at, and created_by cost nothing to add up front.
cards.body: They're brutally expensive to backfill accurately once that history is already lost.

cards.heading: Normalize by default, denormalize with a reason
cards.hook: Third normal form is the right starting point for almost every table.
cards.body: Denormalizing a column should answer a measured slow query, never a guess made in advance.

cards.heading: TEXT over an arbitrary VARCHAR limit
cards.hook: PostgreSQL stores TEXT and VARCHAR identically on disk — a VARCHAR(255) limit buys you nothing except a violation the day someone needs 256 characters.

cards.heading: Atomicity means no partial transfers
cards.hook: BEGIN and COMMIT around a debit and a credit guarantee that if the credit fails, the debit rolls back too.
cards.body: Money can never vanish from one account without appearing in the other.

cards.heading: Isolation decides what you can see mid-flight
cards.hook: Without isolation, one transaction can read another's half-finished work before it even commits — a dirty read.

cards.heading: Read Committed is the practical default
cards.hook: PostgreSQL's default takes a fresh snapshot per statement, so a transaction sees new commits between its own steps.
cards.body: Fits most web application workloads without needing to be touched.

cards.heading: Serializable is for when correctness can't bend
cards.hook: Serializable detects and aborts transactions that couldn't have run in any real serial order.
cards.body: Costly, but the right call for a bank transfer or an inventory reservation.

cards.heading: Pessimistic vs optimistic locking
cards.hook: FOR UPDATE locks a row at read time and makes everyone else wait.
cards.body: Optimistic locking just checks a version number and retries on conflict instead of blocking.
cards.code:
UPDATE orders SET total = 600, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 123 AND version = 4;

cards.heading: Deadlocks come from inconsistent lock order
cards.hook: Lock row 1 then 2 while another locks 2 then 1, and both wait forever.
cards.body: Always acquire locks in the same order, and the deadlock simply can't happen.

cards.heading: SKIP LOCKED makes a simple job queue
cards.hook: Every worker grabs the next unlocked job instantly instead of queueing behind whoever got there first.
cards.code:
SELECT * FROM jobs ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

cards.heading: Savepoints allow a partial rollback
cards.hook: A SAVEPOINT lets you roll back just the failed part of a transaction without discarding everything else already done.

cards.heading: Two-phase commit has a weak point
cards.hook: If the coordinator crashes between prepare and commit, every participant is left holding its locks with no one to tell it what happened.

cards.heading: The Saga pattern replaces one big transaction
cards.hook: A saga runs local transactions in sequence, each with its own compensating action ready if a later step fails.

cards.heading: synchronize: true belongs in development only
cards.hook: In production it means a code change can silently alter your live schema with no migration, no rollback, no review.

cards.heading: Migrations are TypeORM's real deployment path
cards.hook: A migration's up applies the change, down reverses it, both committed to git and run as a deliberate step.

cards.heading: Eager loading vs explicit loading
cards.hook: An eager relation loads on every single query whether you need it or not.
cards.body: Naming it explicitly in relations loads it only where it's actually needed.

cards.heading: The N+1 trap hides inside a simple loop
cards.hook: await post.user inside a loop looks harmless but fires one query per post.
cards.code: await postRepository.find({ relations: ['user'] }); // single JOIN

cards.heading: Soft delete needs a DeleteDateColumn
cards.hook: softDelete sets a timestamp instead of removing the row, and every normal find silently excludes it.
cards.code:
await userRepository.softDelete({ id: 1 });
await userRepository.find({ withDeleted: true });

cards.heading: The query builder for anything find can't express
cards.hook: Joins across several relations, raw aggregation, or a subquery in SELECT — the query builder handles what find options can't.

cards.heading: A transaction wraps related writes together
cards.hook: AppDataSource.transaction's manager scopes every save in the callback to one transaction — all succeed, or all roll back.

cards.heading: Batch insert beats one row at a time
cards.hook: repository.insert with an array issues one multi-row INSERT instead of paying the round trip cost per row.

cards.heading: A unique violation is not a generic error
cards.hook: Catching error.code 23505 and turning it into email already exists beats leaking a raw stack trace to the user.

cards.heading: SQL describes what, not how
cards.hook: A SELECT says what result you want, not the steps to get it — the execution order is entirely the planner's call.

cards.heading: An UPDATE never changes a row in place
cards.hook: PostgreSQL inserts a brand new tuple and marks the old one superseded — the one decision that makes the rest of MVCC possible.

cards.heading: xmin and xmax decide what you can see
cards.hook: Every tuple carries the id of the transaction that created it, and the one that replaced it.
cards.body: A reader's snapshot uses those two numbers to pick the exact right version.

cards.heading: Why readers never block writers
cards.hook: A long read and a concurrent write are just looking at different tuple versions of the same row — neither ever waits for the other.

cards.heading: Dead tuples are the price of lock-free concurrency
cards.hook: A superseded tuple sits as a dead tuple until VACUUM reclaims it — heavy updates without vacuuming pile these up into table bloat.

cards.heading: The isolation level decides when a snapshot is taken
cards.hook: Read Committed snapshots every statement, Repeatable Read snapshots the whole transaction once — same MVCC, different snapshot policy.

cards.heading: Every query passes through the same four stages
cards.hook: Parser, rewriter, planner, executor — every query, whether it takes a microsecond or an hour.

cards.heading: Constraints aren't just validation
cards.hook: A NOT NULL constraint lets the planner skip null-checking logic entirely — the planner reads your constraints too.

cards.heading: The planner picks the join algorithm, not you
cards.hook: Nested loop, hash join, or merge join — chosen from table size, indexes, and statistics, never from how you wrote the query.

cards.heading: A CTE is no longer an optimization fence
cards.hook: Since Postgres 12, a plain WITH query gets inlined just like a subquery would.
cards.body: Write WITH x AS MATERIALIZED when you deliberately want it to run once, in isolation.

cards.heading: LATERAL does top N per group cleanly
cards.hook: Most recent order per customer becomes a plain LIMIT 1 inside a LATERAL subquery — no window function needed.
cards.code:
LATERAL (
  SELECT total_cents FROM orders o
  WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
  ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1
)

cards.heading: Correlated vs uncorrelated subqueries
cards.hook: An uncorrelated subquery runs once, standalone — a correlated one conceptually runs once per outer row.

cards.heading: FILTER applies to just one aggregate
cards.hook: One query, several differently-filtered totals, no self join needed.
cards.code:
count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid,
count(*) AS total

cards.heading: NOT IN with a nullable subquery returns nothing
cards.hook: If that subquery can return even one NULL, the whole NOT IN silently returns zero rows.
cards.body: NOT EXISTS doesn't have this trap and is almost always the safer choice.

cards.heading: An unindexed foreign key slows every delete
cards.hook: PostgreSQL never auto-indexes the referencing side of a foreign key — deleting triggers a full scan to check for orphans.

cards.heading: RANK leaves gaps, DENSE_RANK doesn't
cards.hook: Two rows tied for first both get RANK 1, then the next jumps to 3 — DENSE_RANK gives them 1 and 2, no gap.

cards.heading: A page is the unit PostgreSQL reads and writes
cards.hook: Every table and index is sliced into fixed 8KB pages — always read or written whole, never partially.

cards.heading: Line pointers let a tuple move safely
cards.hook: A small line pointer array tracks each tuple's offset, so PostgreSQL can shuffle data inside a page without breaking anything pointing at it.

cards.heading: Oversized values get moved out of line
cards.hook: Past roughly 2KB, large columns get compressed and moved into a separate TOAST table automatically.
cards.body: Which is also why selecting a wide jsonb column you don't need can cost more than it looks like it should.

cards.heading: shared_buffers is PostgreSQL's page cache
cards.hook: A requested page checks memory first and only hits disk on a miss — a clock-sweep algorithm decides what to evict.

cards.heading: A SELECT can trigger a write
cards.hook: The first read after a bulk load caches each tuple's commit status directly on the page — a read that surprisingly writes to disk.

cards.heading: Durability lives in pg_wal
cards.hook: Every change hits the write-ahead log before the matching page is touched in memory.
cards.body: Crash before the page saves, and replaying the log from the last checkpoint loses nothing.

cards.heading: The catalog is just another heap table
cards.hook: pg_class and every system catalog use the exact same page and tuple layout as any table you create.
cards.body: Which is why you can query them with plain SQL, just like anything else.

cards.heading: A table's filename is not its name
cards.hook: A table's file is named by its relfilenode, not its table name.
cards.body: TRUNCATE, CLUSTER, and VACUUM FULL swap in a fresh file while the table's identity stays exactly the same.
